# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical Reading: Two-Year Follow-up of Varden County and the Halden Subset

**Bottom line:** This is a strong follow-up that tackles the open questions directly: persistence, the meetings mechanism, and unrecorded hours. It does so with randomised comparison, a second hours measure and a pre-registered mediation test. Its core finding, a smaller but persistent per-hour gain of about 8–10% in case-processing, is well supported. Several claims are stated more firmly than the evidence allows:

- The summary compares figures from two different hours measures.
- The "decline" is not statistically distinguishable from no change, and part of it may come from control offices improving.
- The meetings test reuses the offices that generated the hypothesis.
- The hours-log measure is not clearly defined, and on its stated definition the hours figures don't reconcile with the fall in meeting time.

## 1. Arithmetic check

**Correct:**
- **Per-hour gains:** 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%, and 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%. The confidence intervals agree with dividing the output-per-FTE interval by the hours ratio, and all are symmetric on the log scale.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Halden subset:** 34.9 / 40.3 gives a 13.4% fall in hours, and 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8%.
- **Counter-office cost estimate:** Restoring output after an 11.4% per-employee loss needs about 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff, so the "12%" figure is consistent. A 12% rise in staff raising cost per contact by 9% implies wages are about 75% of total cost. That is plausible but unstated.

**Problem 1: the summary compares different measures.**
- The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% uses timesheets and 8.5% uses system logs.
- The like-for-like timesheet comparison is 12.5% to 9.8%, which the body itself calls the right comparison.
- The summary therefore overstates the decline: about 22% of the gain on the same measure, against about 32% across measures.
- Section 5's "about a quarter" is also closer to the like-for-like figure, so the summary is inconsistent with the paper's own text.

**Problem 2: the log measure doesn't reconcile with the meeting cut.**
- The logs are said to record time "working on cases." If so, they exclude meetings.
- Relative to control, timesheet hours fell about 12%, or roughly 4.5 hours from 37.9. Meetings fell about 3.3 hours relative to control.
- That leaves non-meeting time falling only about 1.2 hours, or about 4%.
- Case-work time should then have fallen by no more than about 4%, yet logs show −11%.
- If the logs actually capture all logged-in time, meetings included, the figures fit, but then "working on cases" is the wrong description.

This matters for two reasons:
- **The "more work" claim.** The paper reads −11% on logs against −12% on timesheets as showing that logs capture slightly more work. If the two measures cover different activities, their percentage changes are not comparable in that way.
- **The mediation result.** If the denominator excludes meeting time, cutting meetings doesn't mechanically raise output per log-hour. A meetings effect on that outcome would then be a stronger finding than one on output per total hour. The report needs to define the measure.

**Minor:** the Halden baseline of 40.3 hours equals the Comment's figure for its 27 time-tracking organisations. It should be the baseline for these 11 specific organisations, unless it happens to coincide.

## 2. What's strong

- **The study the field needed:** randomised, record-based output, two hours measures, 24 months, and an analysis registered at month 11, before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- **A mediation analysis set up properly:** the outcome is specified in advance, two mediators are registered, and the unexplained share (35%) is reported rather than hidden.
- **Baseline meeting data now exist:** treated offices went from 7.4 to 3.9 hours and control offices from 7.2 to 7.0. This answers my earlier concern that the month-six gap might reflect a chance imbalance at baseline. The groups were balanced, and the fall happened in treated offices.
- **Coverage-bound work is resolved decisively:** the counter arm was ended over waiting times, and the report now includes a control comparison (7.3 vs 4.0 minutes) and a cost estimate.
- **It checks the meta-analysis's long-term studies:** the four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. This confirms the concern I raised about that duration analysis and correctly removes it as evidence against decay.
- **Appropriate caution elsewhere:** the unplanned meeting-audit observation is handled carefully, the Halden survivors are explicitly labelled as such, and the limitations include the mediation assumption.

## 3. Issues

### a. The "decline" may not be real, and may partly come from control offices

- **Statistical overlap.** The 9-month interval (+6.9 to +18.4) and the 24-month timesheet interval (+4.6 to +15.2) overlap heavily. The data are consistent with modest decay, or with none at all.
- **Control offices changed.** Two control offices cut meetings in month 15 and gained 4.1% per hour. Averaged over the seven control offices, that is about 1.2 points, which accounts for nearly half of the 2.7-point fall in the difference-in-differences estimate.
- **What the decline means.** Some of the apparent decline therefore reflects control offices improving, not treated offices fading.
- **What can be said.** The per-hour gain persisted at about 9–10% on timesheets. Whether it declined is uncertain.
- **How this affects the critics.** The response to the meta-analysis still stands: its four long studies can't show "no decay," and this study can't show decay either. The response to the Comment also stands, because the gain clearly did not reach zero.

The control-office meeting figures look slightly odd. Two of the seven offices fell by 2.1 hours each, yet the control average fell only 0.2. That implies the other five rose by about 0.5 hours on average. This is possible but worth reporting.

### b. The meetings confirmation is not independent

- The hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices, through the month-six correlation (r = 0.71).
- The registered test was filed at month 11, after the 9-month results were known, and uses the same offices.
- Registration prevents analytic flexibility, but it does not create a new sample.
- "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't help much. Repeated months from the same 14 offices are not independent, so the effective sample is still about 14 clusters.
- The Comment's specific charge, a post hoc story fitted to a subgroup, is weakened: the effect held in a pre-specified model with baseline data. But this is confirmation within the same units, not replication.

### c. The mediation estimates look precise for 14 clusters

- **Narrow intervals.** A share-of-effect interval of 28–66% is a ratio whose denominator, the total gain, is itself uncertain (+3.4 to +13.8). With 14 offices, I would expect a wider interval. The report should state how clustering was handled, for example with a cluster bootstrap.
- **Causal assumptions.** Mediation shares rest on strong assumptions, which the report rightly flags.
- **Overlapping mediators.** Fewer meetings could themselves reduce fatigue, so the two mediators aren't cleanly separable.
- **Scale of the effect.** "47%" amounts to about 4 percentage points of an 8.5% gain.

### d. The Halden reversions don't split as cleanly as stated

- One of the three reversions was a marketing agency, which the meta-analysis would code as discretionary work.
- It cited client deadlines. That is a third kind of constraint, responsiveness to external timing, which is neither coverage nor flexible backlog.
- The summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" stretches to cover it.
- This suggests the discretionary/coverage-bound distinction needs a middle category.

### e. The Halden subset is selected at several stages

- The 23 organisations with records were already a selected group.
- Of those, 9 didn't respond. Non-responders may well have done worse, but the report doesn't consider this.
- Calling the 11.8% gain an "upper bound" is too strong a term. It is likely an overestimate for organisations in general, but without a comparison group it isn't formally bounded.
- Notably, 11.8% is still close to the Varden estimate, which modestly supports the gain being real in discretionary settings.

### f. Smaller points

- **The month-15 meeting audit.** This is a before-after comparison in two offices that chose to act, so there may be regression to the mean and selection. The report says this.
- **Strawman in the rebuttal.** The Comment extrapolated self-reported energy in Halden survivors, not output in Varden. Saying the Varden result is "not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" is fair, but it is somewhat stronger than what the Comment actually claimed.
- **Authorship.** A Halden author co-writes a rebuttal touching on Halden's critics, and the trial team is evaluating its own trial. Neither is improper, and the registration mitigates it, but it's worth noting given this is a field report and not peer reviewed.
- **Persistent fatigue improvement.** Fatigue scores remained 0.34 SD better than control at 24 months. This contrasts with the fading energy scores in Halden, though the measures differ.

## 4. Assessment of the report's claims

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A per-hour gain persists at 24 months (about 8.5–9.8%) | **Well supported.** This is the strongest evidence to date. |
| The gain fell from 12.5% to 8.5% | **Overstated.** It mixes measures; like-for-like is 12.5% to 9.8%, with overlapping intervals and possible control-office contamination. |
| Logs show slightly more work than timesheets | **Unclear** until the log measure is defined. |
| Meetings explain 47% of the gain | **Supported as within-sample confirmation**, but not an independent replication, and the interval is possibly too narrow. |
| Fatigue explains 18% | **Supported**, with the same caveats. |
| The Comment's "entirely an artifact" is refuted | **Yes.** |
| The meta-analysis's "no decay" is unsupported | **Yes.** But decay isn't established either. |
| Halden reversions were all coverage-bound | **Partly.** One was a client-deadline case in discretionary work. |
| Reorganisation alone might capture part of the gain | **Suggestive only**, as the authors say. |

## 5. Where the five documents now leave things

| Question | Best current answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | **About 8–12%, lasting at least 24 months.** Varden (8.5–9.8%), the Halden survivors (11.8%) and the review's controlled estimate (9.6%) all agree. |
| Output per worker, discretionary | **Slightly below control (about −2% to −3%).** Intervals allow a loss of up to about 8%. The hours cut is mostly but not fully offset. |
| Coverage-bound work | **Settled: output and service fall.** Restoring service costs about 9% more per contact, and the county ended the counter arm. |
| Client-deadline work | **A possible third category.** The evidence is a single reversion. |
| Decay | **Possibly modest, not established.** It did not fall to zero, and control contamination complicates the estimate. |
| Mechanism | **Meetings are the largest identified pathway** (about half), with fatigue smaller (about a fifth) and a third unexplained. This needs replication in new offices. |
| Can reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | **The key open question.** It needs a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours. |
| Sick leave and retention | **Consistently better, about 27–30% fewer sick days, with randomised support.** |
| Cost | **Known only for counter work.** Case-processing overtime cost is still unreported. |

The most useful next study would be a three-arm trial in new organisations: reduced hours, reorganisation without reduced hours (meeting audit, protected focus time), and control. That design would replicate the meetings finding in an independent sample. It would also test whether the gain needs shorter hours or only the changes that shorter hours force.
